accuracy.evidence: Every worked result was recomputed by hand: (2 + 3i)(4 − i) = 8 − 2i + 12i − 3i² = 11 + 10i; i(3 + i) = −1 + 3i and i(−1 + 3i) = −3 − i; (1 + i)(2 + 2i) = 4i with |z||w| = √2 × 2√2 = 4 and 45° + 45° = 90°; all six sorter cards and six challenge items (e.g. (1 + 2i)(3 + i) = 1 + 7i, (2 + i)(2 − i) = 5). Spec references checked: Edexcel 9FM0 Core Pure 1 sections 2.1 and 2.3 and AQA 7367; the general product (ac − bd) + (ad + bc)i matches the specification formula.

misconceptions.evidence: Distractors are built from the known slips, each computed so the wrong answer is exactly what the slip produces: i² = +1 (5 + 10i, 5 + 7i, 3), pairwise multiplication ac + bdi (8 − 3i, 3 + 2i), the minus applied only to the real part ((4 + 3i) − (1 − 2i) = 3 + i, 3 − 2i), sign slips in addition (4 + 7i), leaving i² unsimplified, and adding moduli (5 instead of 6).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagcxops is about operations, not the number system: the sum appears as w's arrow on z's tip, the difference as the arrow from w to z, × i animates a 90° rotation with a trail, a four-cell product grid needs i² = −1 applied as a separate act, and the final scene reads |z||w| and arg z + arg w live as w moves. flagcplx (Re, Im, set membership, equality) and flagcxroot (discriminant, conjugate roots) do none of these; source similarity is under 30% to both and all other labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners find w = 3 + 2i and w = 3 + 5i themselves by dragging, so component-wise addition and the sign change in subtraction are discovered from the readout before the done message states them; two presses of × i show i² = −1 as a half turn; the grid forces all four products before simplification; finding w for zw = 4i makes the modulus product and angle sum visible.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options: w = 7 + 4i (adding z instead of undoing it), (4 + 3i) − (1 − 2i) = 3 + i (minus only on the real part, the most common subtraction slip), and moduli add. Each is disproved by the target the learner must hit on the diagram.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six why() messages name the exact slip: sign slip in addition, i² left unsimplified (keepi), minus not distributed (minus), i² treated as +1 (plus1), cross terms dropped (cross), and moduli added (modadd). The grid scene adds three more specific messages: a cell taken as a sum, a sign error, and a lost i.

readability.evidence: Learner paragraphs use short sentences with one rule each and a worked example straight after it; notation is standard A level (a + bi, i², Argand diagram, modulus, argument). validate_lessons.py readability passes for the learner text; the adult text was split into shorter sentences after it first measured grade 12.2 and now passes.

no_filler.evidence: Each learner paragraph covers one operation (add, subtract, multiply) or the geometry; adult paragraphs give the specification, the single new step i² = −1, five named mistakes and the lab tasks. The content gate found no filler phrases and under 12% overlap with the complex number system and complex roots lessons.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px screenshots in light and dark: the Argand square fills the width with ±6 axes at about 28 px per unit, lattice snapping and a 22 px hit radius make w easy to drag, point labels stay inside the square, the grid cells are about 120 by 60 px, and the answer tiles are 64 px tall. After the check the rotating arrow was redrawn above its label so it is not hidden.

accessibility.evidence: Re ±1 and Im ±1 buttons move w with no dragging, × i is a button, and every grid cell and final answer has a button. Each change updates the canvas aria-label and the live region with the full equation (for example 'w = 3 + 2i, z + w = 5 + 3i. On target.'). walk.cjs ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA on desktop and iPhone 13 in both themes with no violations; point colours switch to lighter tints on the dark plane.
